Location surfaces from detection counts

Source: R/likelihood.R
location_surface.Rd

For each animal and time bin, computes the posterior probability that the animal was in each water cell of the field's grid, given which receivers were listening and how many detections each logged. The surface is the likelihood of the bin's counts in each water cell under a flat prior over the water cells, normalised to sum to one over them. It is therefore a posterior by Bayes' rule. The default likelihood is binomial and uses the detections and the misses (binomial grid localization). With likelihood = "presence_only" it is the product of the detection probabilities of the detections alone (presence-only grid localization). Each bin is computed on its own; no movement model links bins.

Usage

location_surface(
  counts,
  field,
  overdispersion = c("station_hour", "none"),
  likelihood = c("binomial", "presence_only"),
  control = list()
)

Arguments

counts

Counts from bin_detections(), or a data frame with the same columns: animal_id, bin_start, bin_end, receiver_serial, y, n and listening. Rows with listening = FALSE are left out. When the field is keyed by station_id and counts has no station_id, each receiver_serial is mapped to its station on the bin's date through the field's deployment lookup, when the field holds one.

field

A detection field (class "de_field"): a list holding eta, the logit of the per-transmission detection probability with one row per water cell and one column per receiver; cells, the grid cell numbers of the rows; receivers, the column names; grid, the raster or the path of a raster file; and model, whose sigma$station_hour sets the overdispersion.

overdispersion

"station_hour" (the default) or "none". Not used when likelihood = "presence_only".

likelihood

"binomial" (the default) or "presence_only"; see Two readings of the curve.

control

A list of settings: cores, the number of processes for animals (default 1; forked processes, so 1 on Windows); nodes, the Gauss-Hermite nodes (default NULL, set from the standard deviation as above); kept_mass, the share of each surface kept (default 0.999); table_step, the logit step of the term tables (default 0.01); on_degenerate, "stop" (default) or "skip"; write_dir, a directory to which each animal's surfaces are written (default NULL, return them); near_m, the radius in metres of near_mass (default NULL, per receiver the farthest cell centre at p >= 0.5; see Details).

Value

A data frame of class "loc_surface" with the columns animal_id, bin_start, cell and prob, one row per kept cell. Its attributes hold bins (one row per animal and bin: bin_end, n_transmissions, n_listening, n_detecting, y_total, log_lik, the log of the mean likelihood over water cells, kept_mass, n_cells, misfit_p, misfit_receiver, mode_cell, mode_dist_m, near_receiver, near_m and near_mass), likelihood (the reading used), overdispersion (form, sigma, nodes), kept (the rule), grid (packed), n_water_cells, receivers (the listening rows used), receiver_xy (receiver coordinates, when the field holds them), skipped (degenerate bins left out: animal, bin and reason) and not_listening_bins (bins left out because all their detections were at receivers not listening: animal, bin and detections).

With control$write_dir, each animal with at least one surface is saved by saveRDS() as a "loc_surface" of its own, and the call returns a data frame with one row per animal: animal_id, file, bins and rows, with the attributes bins, overdispersion, skipped and not_listening_bins as above.

Details

The model. In bin \(t\), an animal in cell \(c\) sends \(n_t\) transmissions, the column n of counts, taken as known. Each listening receiver's count is binomial in \(n_t\) with the field's detection probability at that cell, the receivers independent given the cell. The surface is the product of these terms over the listening receivers, normalised over every water cell of the grid, including cells no receiver can hear: a flat prior over water. Silent receivers count: a receiver that heard nothing makes the cells near it less likely. The article Hourly positions against the true track writes the model out and explains how \(n_t\) is set, in its section The model: https://jakebrownscombe.github.io/detfield/articles/positioning.html#the-model.

The model makes six assumptions. The animal stays in one cell for the bin. The tag sits at the cell centre, and its depth is ignored. Each receiver's detection probability is constant within the bin. The field is known. Transmissions are detected independently given the cell. Every detection is a true transmission of this tag, with no false detections or code collisions. A receiver whose deployment covers at least min_cover of the bin (0.5 by default in bin_detections()) is taken to listen for all of it, so it counts every transmission of the bin. With blocked = 0 in de_model(), the clear-line curve is read across land; de_field() gives the count of such pairs in a message.

Two readings of the curve. likelihood = "binomial", the default, is binomial grid localization: each listening receiver's count is binomial in the transmissions sent, so its misses and the silence of other receivers are evidence too. It is the binomial count model of Winton et al. (2018) with the detection function fixed in advance rather than estimated, on a grid of water cells rather than in continuous space. Winton et al. take the number of trials as the maximum expected number of transmissions in the interval, and note that a Poisson count may suit tags whose transmission intervals are programmed to vary, as random delays are. In the terms of Hostetter and Royle (2020) it is independent localization of one bin, with all the bin's transmissions sent from one position. They describe fixing the detection function from a range test as the common practice, and recommend estimating the detection parameters from the telemetry data instead.

Use the binomial reading by default. It places an animal that one receiver heard rarely on the ring of cells where that receiver's probability matches its count. Its credible regions are calibrated when the curve is right for tagged animals at the bin scale and the animal stays in one cell for the bin. In the example study the curve is the one that drew the detections, but the animals swim within the hour: the 95% regions held 35.3% of the true minutes and the hour's mean true position in 156 of 212 hours (74%). The article Hourly positions against the true track computes both, in its section Credible regions and their coverage: https://jakebrownscombe.github.io/detfield/articles/positioning.html.

likelihood = "presence_only" is presence-only grid localization: the log-likelihood of cell \(c\) is \(\sum_s y_{st} \log p_s(c)\), the product of \(p_s(c)\) over the detections, with misses and silent receivers dropped. It never places an animal away from the receivers that heard it; use it as a check when the curve's level is not trusted. Its credible regions are not calibrated: the surface narrows as the count grows, whatever the curve's level. On the example data (stoney_track, 212 detected hours of five animals, 12,720 minutes), its 95% regions held the animal's true cell in 23.8% of the minutes, against 35.3% for the binomial reading; neither reaches 95% there, because the animals move within the hour. Compare its region sizes between bins only. Under it overdispersion does not apply, and "station_hour" is ignored with a warning. misfit_p and the near diagnostics are computed against the binomial prediction under either reading.

Overdispersion. Detection probability varies between receivers and hours more than a range curve says. With overdispersion = "station_hour", each receiver-bin carries its own logit-scale effect, normal with standard deviation field$model$sigma$station_hour, which is integrated out by Gauss-Hermite quadrature. This standard deviation is the whole spread of one receiver's logit about the curve within one bin, with all sources of variation combined.

"station_hour" is the default. It applies the spread when the field's model gives a standard deviation above 0, and runs as the plain binomial when it gives 0. When the model gives none, as de_model() and de_logistic() do by default, the call stops. This is why every example sets sigma = list(station_hour = 0) in de_model().

The standard deviation is defined only together with the curve it was estimated around. Paired with a curve that is too flat or too low at the bin scale, a large standard deviation lets a strong count be explained from far away, and the surface moves away from the receivers that heard the animal. Estimate the curve and the standard deviation together, from data at the bin scale (for example range-test windows of the bin length), and pass both; a value estimated around one curve does not transfer to another. A value that is too small for its curve makes regions too small. The form also assumes the effect is normal on the logit scale. When the truth differs, for example when a receiver either hears the tag in an hour or does not, regions can hold the truth less often than their level.

The standard deviation is a property of the detection model and is never estimated here. It describes hour bins: under "station_hour", the default, with a standard deviation above 0, a warning says so when a bin is not an hour. With "none" the receivers' counts are independent binomials, which is overconfident whenever detection varies between hours.

Computation. All sums are in log space, so a bin with thousands of transmissions and no detection stays finite. Under "station_hour" each receiver's term is read from a table over the logit, built once per count and number of transmissions by adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature, which transforms the variable of integration so the nodes sample the integrand where its mass lies (Liu and Pierce 1994), and interpolated by cubic Hermite polynomials with exact derivatives. The number of nodes grows with the standard deviation (25 per logit, from 20 to 200). The script https://github.com/jakebrownscombe/detfield/blob/main/validation/02_quadrature_error.R compares each term with numerical integration over counts 0 to n, for n of 30, 60 and 720. It is in the repository and not in the installed package. The largest error in log probability is 1.2e-6 at a standard deviation of 2.55, 6.0e-6 at 3.4 and 1.1e-4 at 6. A smaller control$nodes gives a warning, because the error grows fast as nodes fall: 20 nodes give 3.2e-4, 1.8e-3 and 1.8e-2 at the same standard deviations. On the example data (stoney_track, 212 detected animal-hours, 4,818 water cells) at a standard deviation of 2.55, surfaces were compared with surfaces from 200 nodes. Surfaces from 1 node were off by up to 0.0339 in total variation, from 20 nodes by up to 1.15e-4, and from the default of 64 nodes by up to 2.43e-7. The script https://github.com/jakebrownscombe/detfield/blob/main/validation/01_node_error.R computes these; it is in the repository and not in the installed package. Above a standard deviation of 8 the 200-node cap applies, also with a warning. Below a logit at which the detection probability is negligible, the term is computed in closed form, so a field with very negative logits costs no more than one without.

Cost. Each call has a fixed cost per animal, for the tables and the silent receivers' terms, before any bin. On the example data at a standard deviation of 2.55, one hour of stoney-01 took 0.17 s and all 43 of its hours took 2.59 s. These are medians of five runs. The script https://github.com/jakebrownscombe/detfield/blob/main/validation/03_location_surface_timing.R prints them; it is in the repository and not in the installed package. Give all of an animal's bins in one call: a call per day pays the fixed cost once a day.

Large runs. The kept cells of every bin come back as one table, and a table holds at most 2,147,483,647 rows. A run that would exceed it stops with a message. With control$write_dir, each animal's surfaces are written to their own file as they are computed, so the session never holds them all; the call then returns a table of the files.

What is kept. Each surface keeps only the smallest set of cells that holds control$kept_mass (default 0.999) of its probability, because every water cell of every bin would not fit in memory for a large array. Probabilities are not rescaled, so they sum to the kept mass.

Misfit. For each bin, misfit_p in the bin table is the smallest, over the receivers that detected the animal, of the posterior predictive probability of logging at least the count that receiver logged, and misfit_receiver names that receiver. A value near zero means no cell of the surface explains that receiver's count under the field: the field may be wrong near that receiver, or the animal moved within the bin.

Distance from the receivers that heard the animal. A surface can fit every count and still sit away from the receivers that logged them. This happens with a curve that is too high near a receiver. A low count is then best explained by a ring of cells at the distance where the curve gives that rate, and misfit_p stays high. Three columns of the bin table show this. mode_dist_m is the straight-line distance from the centre of the most probable cell to the nearest receiver that detected the animal in the bin. near_mass is the probability within near_m metres (straight line) of near_receiver, the receiver that logged the most detections in the bin (the first in row order on a tie). near_m is control$near_m when given; otherwise it is the longest clear-line distance (in_water) from that receiver to a water cell centre at which the field's detection probability is still 0.5 or more, read from the field's distance table. Because it is read off cell centres, it falls short of the curve's d50 by up to one cell diagonal. On the example data it is 224 m for receiver S069, whose curve gives d50 253 m at its depth of 1.2 m. Where the field holds no distance table, or the receiver has no such pair, near_m and near_mass are NA; set control$near_m. near_mass is computed over every water cell, before cells are dropped by kept_mass. Distances are in the units of the grid's CRS, metres for any grid water_distances() accepts. print() counts the bins with near_mass below 0.001.

Checks. A surface that is not a distribution is degenerate: a log-likelihood that is NaN, zero likelihood in every cell, or the same likelihood in every cell. By default it stops the run with the animal and bin named; with control$on_degenerate = "skip", the bin is left out, recorded in the attribute skipped, and a warning gives the count.

Matching receivers. Rows of counts match columns of field by receiver_serial; when the field's columns are stations, by station_id. A listening receiver with no column in the field stops the run, because leaving it out would drop its evidence without notice. Every cell of the field must be a water cell (not NA) of its grid.

Detections at receivers not listening. Rows with listening = FALSE are left out. A bin whose detections all sit on such rows is left out as well, because without them it would be computed as a bin in which every listening receiver was silent, which puts the animal away from every receiver. Such bins are counted in a warning and listed in the attribute not_listening_bins.

References

Hostetter, N. J. and Royle, J. A. (2020). Movement-assisted localization from acoustic telemetry data. Movement Ecology, 8, 15. doi:10.1186/s40462-020-00199-6

Liu, Q. and Pierce, D. A. (1994). A note on Gauss-Hermite quadrature. Biometrika, 81, 624-629. doi:10.1093/biomet/81.3.624

Winton, M. V., Kneebone, J., Zemeckis, D. R. and Fay, G. (2018). A spatial point process model to estimate individual centres of activity from passive acoustic telemetry data. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 9, 2262-2272. doi:10.1111/2041-210X.13080

See also

bin_detections() for the counts; credible_region() and sample_locations() for what to do with the surfaces.

Examples

# Stoney Lake: a detection field from distances through water, the
# detections counted per hour, and one surface per detected hour.
tif <- system.file("extdata", "stoney_depth.tif", package = "detfield")
grid <- terra::rast(tif)
# Beyond 2 km the Stoney curve is below 0.001 at every receiver; leaving
# those pairs out keeps the example quick.
dist <- water_distances(grid, stoney_track$receivers,
                        max_distance = 2000)
model <- de_logistic(d50 = c(250, 750), d05 = c(500, 1500), depth = c(1, 35))
field <- de_field(dist, de_model(model, sigma = list(station_hour = 0)))
#> 194 of 7,669 receiver-cell pairs with p >= 0.05 have land on the
#>   straight line between them; with blocked = 0 the curve is read on
#>   them as if the line were clear. See `blocked` in ?de_model.
counts <- bin_detections(stoney_track$detections, stoney_track$receivers,
                         stoney_track$tags)
surface <- location_surface(counts, field)
surface
#> Location surface: 5 animals, 212 bins, 5,934 cells kept in all
#> Cells kept per bin: median 19 of 4,818 water cells (range 6 to 220)
#> Likelihood: binomial (detections and misses at every listening
#>   receiver)
#> Spread: none (overdispersion = "none")
#> Each bin keeps the smallest set of cells holding 0.999 of its
#>   probability
#> Misfit: 10 of 212 bins have a detecting receiver whose count the
#>   surface gives a chance below 0.01
#> Near: 47 of 212 bins put under 0.001 of their probability within 223.6
#>   to 447.2 m of the receiver with the most detections (per receiver,
#>   its farthest cell centre at p >= 0.5)
#> Modes sit a median 316 m (max 707 m) from the nearest detecting
#>   receiver, over 212 bins
#>   animal_id           bin_start cell       prob
#> 1 stoney-01 2024-06-01 04:00:00 2502 0.11482306
#> 2 stoney-01 2024-06-01 04:00:00 2836 0.11203616
#> 3 stoney-01 2024-06-01 04:00:00 2669 0.10675649
#> 4 stoney-01 2024-06-01 04:00:00 2670 0.08254470
#> 5 stoney-01 2024-06-01 04:00:00 2837 0.08173242
#> 6 stoney-01 2024-06-01 04:00:00 2334 0.07061498
bins <- attr(surface, "bins")
head(bins[, c("animal_id", "bin_start", "n_cells", "misfit_p", "mode_dist_m")])
#>   animal_id           bin_start n_cells     misfit_p mode_dist_m
#> 1 stoney-01 2024-06-01 04:00:00      38 0.5264966814    447.2136
#> 2 stoney-01 2024-06-01 05:00:00       8 0.3541473904    282.8427
#> 3 stoney-01 2024-06-01 06:00:00       9 0.3277769506    424.2641
#> 4 stoney-01 2024-06-01 07:00:00      12 0.3660876826    223.6068
#> 5 stoney-01 2024-06-01 08:00:00       9 0.0001923432    316.2278
